text: They didn't just throw it at a moon and hope for the best. Cassini was aimed to plunge through Saturn's atmosphere, where it would burn up, and that was the whole point of the final orbit. You could try to land it on Enceladus or Titan, but then you're bringing a piece of spacecraft that sat near Earth for decades, and there's a tiny risk of hitchhiking microbes or dust. Burning it up avoids that. A moon's surface stays cleaner, and any future mission won't have to worry about a dead probe sitting there. I'd say it's the cheap insurance policy for planetary protection.

It's probably not that your leg is truly doing nothing. On a skateboard, the leg you're not pushing with is still holding you upright and keeping the board steady. That's a lot of quiet work, especially if your stance is off. So if that leg hurts, I'd first look at how you're standing. Are your knees locked? Are your ankles stiff? If your feet are too close together, or you're leaning the wrong way, the non-pushing leg has to compensate, and that can strain the calf or the Achilles. It can also load your hip. When you push, your center of mass shifts, and the leg that isn't pushing takes some of the load as you recover. I'm not a doctor, so I won't call it anything specific, but I've seen people assume one leg is just along for the ride when in fact it's doing all the balancing. Try relaxing your knees, spreading your feet to about shoulder-width, and keeping your center of gravity low. If the hurt is in the shin, it's often from the board's wheels or your stance. If it's in the hip or groin, that's more about how you lean and twist. You might also have a tight hamstring or a slightly uneven stance. And when you push, the pushing leg does the work, but the stationary leg absorbs the little jolts from the ground. Skateboards are rough on the joints if your form is bad. If it's a dull ache after riding, that's different from a sharp pain that comes on while you're pushing. The dull one usually means your legs are absorbing more vibration than they should. If the pain doesn't settle after you adjust your stance, or if it comes back every time you ride, I'd have it looked at by someone who knows, because a real problem could be hiding behind the soreness.

A lot of the confusion comes from treating the word African like a passport, when it's really about ancestry. Most Black Americans didn't step off a boat last month, and plenty have families here for generations, but their families usually trace some roots to West or Central Africa. That's the thread the name is picking up. It's the same way we call Americans of Italian, Irish or Polish descent by those nationalities, even if their great grandfathers were born in Boston or Philadelphia. The label doesn't mean everyone left a country called Africa recently. In practice, the name groups people by shared history and social experience, not by where they were born. That's why you can be born and raised in Georgia or Ohio and still be called African American.

Also, not all Black Americans are ethnically African in the way people imagine. Some have mixed heritage, and some identify as Black through culture and community rather than a single birthplace. So African American is more of a historical and cultural marker than a travel record. If you meet someone and assume they can tell you exactly which African country their ancestor came from, you're putting a finer point on the label than it's meant to carry.

It's rarely one big source. Factions get guns from captured army warehouses, border smugglers coming through Lebanon or Iraq, and dealers who keep weapons moving from country to country. Sometimes a neighboring state or local militia quietly hands over crates, and sometimes arms dealers make money by selling to whoever can pay. They still get them because the fighting hasn't stopped. Even if a truce holds for a while, each side wants enough rifles, grenades, and ammunition to keep its position, deter an attack, and be ready if the other side restarts firing. So the supply chains keep running.

You're not being irrational for wanting the high without the cost. If the goal is intense pleasure, the body and brain start adjusting. The same pleasure response that makes a dose feel so good gets less responsive, so you need more to get back to that first feeling. This is not just getting used to it in a casual way. It changes how the system works.

I'd be less focused on the word bad and more on what actually goes wrong in real life. One drug might not ruin your liver, but it can wreck your sleep, your appetite, your relationships, your motivation. Euphoria is a big hit to the pleasure part of the brain, and that part has to deal with the hit. After the drug wears off, the system is kind of running on low, and that low point is what drives the next dose. You can get caught in a loop, and that's where the badness shows up, not in some single side effect.

There's also the stuff nobody thinks about, your heart rate, your blood pressure, your ability to judge danger. Even when the drug itself isn't poisoning you, the behaviour it produces can be the harm. Taking more than you planned because the high is so good, missing work, missing people, spending money you shouldn't. The adverse effect isn't always a classic symptom, and sometimes it's just the life that gets pulled off-centre.

I don't think zero adverse effects is possible if the pleasure is intense. If a drug hits the pleasure part hard, the brain doesn't stay exactly where it was. It changes, and it wants to keep the new state stable. That's why 0 adverse effects sounds like a magic drug. The body treats the change as something to resist, and that resistance is the cost. For some people the cost is mild, for others it's severe, and you can't tell in advance which you'll be.

So yeah, the reason all drugs seem bad is that the very thing making them appealing is also what makes the system shift. You can design something that gives a strong high and is safer for the body, but you can't make the brain completely ignore the change. That's the trade-off, and I think that's what people don't like to hear. That cost is why a perfectly safe, perfectly pleasurable drug is so hard to imagine.

Hi Mike,

That sounds really familiar, and yes, it’s real. Long shopping days are more than just walking. You’re on your feet for hours, constantly stopping, turning, crouching to look at things. The combination of tiredness, poor sleep, and being stuck next to someone who keeps moving can make the head and shoulders ache in a way that’s different from an ordinary headache. I’d bet your neck and back are part of it. Even if you don’t feel sore, your body is still working. I know you’re tired enough already, and it’s not in your head.

Thanks,
Dan

Hi,
Thanks for writing about this. What happened is not a mistake, it’s your mind taking the easy route. Saying “silk” over and over makes that word and its sound stick around, and when your brother threw the cow question at you, the first association your brain grabbed was milk. Cows and milk are paired together in everyday language so strongly that it jumped out before you could check the factual answer. You probably knew it was water, but the quick prompt and the repeated word left you in that automatic mode. If he had asked you what milk is made from, you might have said cow again. The pair is just too close in your memory. I’ve had the same thing happen to me with silly repeated phrases. It’s a funny little mental short-circuit, not something to be embarrassed about. Don’t give it too much thought.
Thanks

Hi,

Yeah, buying a house means a massive amount of paperwork and money moving around. I think the thing you should focus on is the physical condition of the place. When you go look at a house, you're pretty much just checking if you like the layout and the light. The formal survey is where you find out if the building is actually sound. You'd want to get that done before you sign anything. It's kind of like when your car makes a weird knocking sound, and you have to figure out if it's just the exhaust or something much worse inside the engine.

I guess the surveyor will check the roof, the pipes, and any damp in the walls. I'd be more worried about hidden water damage than the peeling paint. It doesn't matter if the kitchen is a bit dated, but a leaky pipe is a real headache. As far as I know, the fees for this add up, so you should budget for those costs right away.

So yeah, get the inspection first, see what's actually wrong with the building, and only then talk to the seller about fixing it or knocking some money off the price. You can always hire a plumber to look at the pipes if the report is too vague.

Thanks

Hi,

It's mostly about what one formula has to do in different places. A normal shampoo is made to clean hair, and a normal bodywash is made to clean skin. A 3-in-1 has to be mild enough for both, so it uses gentler soaps and a bit of conditioner, so you can wash your whole body with it without stripping your hair or skin.

That's the main difference from the individual products. It's not doing each job as well as a dedicated shampoo, bodywash, or conditioner, but it's there so you don't have to carry three bottles.

A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner is narrower: it cleans and conditions hair in one step, but it's not intended to replace bodywash. A 3-in-1 extends that idea to your skin too.

I'd say the 3-in-1 is a convenience product. You'll find it less targeted, and it's usually aimed at travel, kids, or people who want fewer bottles, but if you have dry hair or sensitive skin, a separate conditioner or bodywash will usually do better. I use them when I'm travelling, because one bottle is easier than three. At home, I still keep a separate shampoo and bodywash, because the all-in-one doesn't lather the same way. But for a quick wash, it does the job.

Thanks

Hi,

You can actually watch a continent move by putting GPS receivers on rocks, bridges, or survey markers and letting them log positions for years. The GPS receivers aren't perfect, so teams use many stations and compare them to a stable reference frame. If a marker drifts a few millimeters a year, that drift is the continent's speed in that direction. It's a bit like watching a wall crack slowly open, except here the crack is measured with satellite positions rather than by eye.

GPS is the main tool, but there are other checks too, like shining lasers at satellites and listening to distant radio sources. Tides and weather have to be corrected out. The whole thing is slow, tedious work, and it's the same kind of evidence that lets people say, for example, that North America and Eurasia are separating by only a couple of centimeters per year. Not a lot, but measurable.

The numbers are small, so you can't just glance at one week's data. You have to keep the receivers running and keep calibrating them. I find the scale a bit weird, because you're tracking something as big as a continent with millimeter precision.

Thanks

When two people are related, they're more likely to carry the same hidden gene variations inherited from a common ancestor. Most people carry a few recessive changes that only show up when a child gets two copies, one from each parent. If the parents are unrelated, the odds that both pass the same one are quite low. If they're related, those odds go up, so a child is more likely to be born with problems that affect brain development, learning, and general health.

That's why inbreeding is linked to lower average IQ in the children. It doesn't mean every child is affected, but it raises the chance of serious recessive problems. It's not about mixing in a simple way. It's about hidden weaknesses becoming active. The science is mostly about recessive genes and the risk that two copies line up in the same child, and that's what shows up in IQ tests.

It isn't that arm injuries are painless. The arm has muscle and fat that absorb impact, and it isn't carrying your body weight or housing the heart and lungs. So a hit, shot, or stab there usually means a bruise, cut, or broken bone, not a direct threat to a vital area.

That changes how your brain rates the pain. A blow to the chest or head feels worse because your body treats injuries near vital organs as more urgent. Much of the difference is also mental, because if it's only the arm, you can still move and look at it, so it feels more manageable.

If the injury hits a bone, major blood vessel, or nerve, it can hurt a lot, so don't assume it's minor just because it's the arm. So the location, what's underneath, and your reaction shape the pain. A bruised arm can still hurt, though.

Carbon monoxide is dangerous mainly because it does not just replace the oxygen you breathe, but sticks to the oxygen-carrying part of your red blood cells much more strongly than oxygen does, and stays there. That leaves less room for oxygen, so your tissues get less than they need. It also messes with the way your cells actually use oxygen. Small amounts can matter, and the first signs may feel like a bad hangover or just being a bit off. You may not notice the air is strange. The gas has no smell or color, so it can sneak up on you.

Carbon dioxide is different. It is the waste gas your body makes all the time, and healthy lungs clear it out constantly. In ordinary outside air, the amount is low enough that breathing it is not poisonous. You can notice it when it builds up in a closed or poorly ventilated room, where it can make you drowsy or dizzy. That is a high concentration situation, not the everyday background level most of us breathe. So CO2 is not harmless in every case. It just usually is not the immediate killer in ordinary air.

CO's danger comes from how it sticks to your oxygen carriers. The effect is not the same as simply running out of oxygen. Even if the air still contains oxygen, your blood cannot deliver as much of it as it should. In places with incomplete burning, such as a gas stove or a car idling in a garage, carbon monoxide is the gas you should be more careful with. A simple alarm helps, because you cannot rely on feeling the air. That is the main difference. A CO alarm can be life saving in rooms with gas appliances near a heater or a fireplace.

If an aircraft hits the ground or stops suddenly, the force can throw our bodies forward. The brace position is what we do to keep that force from turning into a serious injury. We bend low, bring our chins toward our chests, and if we can, hold the back of the seat in front of us. Keeping our heads supported and our bodies low reduces the chance of hitting the seatback, floor, or the person ahead of us. It also gives our arms and chest a way to share the impact instead of letting the neck or internal organs take it all.

When the crew calls brace, we move into the position quickly and stay low, chin near the chest, holding the seat back or our legs if instructed. That matters because an emergency can involve more than one jolt. The position won't make a crash feel safe, but it helps spread the force over our bodies. It gives the body somewhere to go, and it keeps our heads and necks from taking the brunt. That's the point, it's a way to manage what happens after the impact, not to avoid the impact itself. That's how we reduce the risk.

It's not that old firms were all wiped out. More often they were tied to local trade, a craft, or a family name, and people remember the trade or the place rather than the brand.

When the industrial era brought railroads, factories and mass markets, companies that could scale or reinvent themselves got attention. Older ones faded into local lore. A few old family shops still exist, but global recognition usually comes from being around long enough to expand. That's why you mainly hear about firms that, as a rule, survived and grew, not the smaller ones that quietly disappeared.

My take is that the dealership's lower rate is often a decoy. The rate is just the interest part, and the dealer can quietly add fees and optional extras that push the total price up. I've seen people pick the lower dealer rate and still end up paying more, because the loan included prep fees, documentation fees, and an extended service contract they didn't actually need. The bank doesn't push those extras on you. It lends against the car at the price you agreed to, and you know the monthly amount before signing.

This is the part I think people miss. A dealer might quote 4.6% on a 60 month loan, but then list a $800 preparation fee and a $400 documentation fee, and ask if you'd like a $2,000 service plan. If you say yes and finance it, your total cost goes up by thousands. The bank might show 5.2%, but you're financing a cleaner number. Over sixty months, the smaller interest rate from the dealer can be wiped out by the add-ons.

There's also the length of the loan. Dealerships can make the payment look small by stretching the term. That lower payment is not the same as lower total interest. If the dealer offers a lower rate but wants you to commit to six years instead of four, you'll pay more in interest even if the percentage is smaller. The bank may offer a slightly higher rate, but a shorter term keeps the total cost lower.

I'd also watch the loan term, because dealerships have an incentive to stretch payments over longer months. The same car can look affordable if the term is 72 months instead of 48, but you're paying interest for a longer stretch. A bank might not sell you a service contract or prep fee, but it also won't hide the payment schedule from you. That's the practical difference. The bank gives you a number you can check against the price, while the dealer can bury the cost in extras.

I'd side with the bank if I were shopping. I want to know the out-the-door price, see every fee in writing, and avoid being upsold into extras I don't want. The dealer's low rate is a strong pitch, but it doesn't prove the deal is the cheap one. The real question isn't which rate looks lower on paper. It's what you actually have to pay by the time the loan is finished.

I think the patchwork of state marijuana law is more confusing than helpful. You can cross into another state with a medical card and suddenly the rules change, like my friend who got stopped at a border with a small baggie of dried flower and was told it was legal in his home state but not necessarily where he was being searched. I get that states get to experiment, but when one state says yes and the next says no, people end up guessing. For me, the problem isn't that marijuana is legal or illegal everywhere. It's the mismatch between what someone can buy in a dispensary and what counts as being high. I've heard too many people treated like a criminal for having a medical card while crossing state lines. I'd rather see the states coordinate so a card actually means something when you drive across a state line.

People keep asking me if the body makes electricity, and I think the answer is simpler than it sounds. It isn't a battery in your chest. Your cells sit across a membrane with more potassium inside and more sodium outside. When a nerve cell decides to fire, tiny gates open, sodium floods in, and the charge flips. That little flip moves down the nerve and makes your fingers twitch or your heart beat. I find that concrete, messy movement more real. You feel it when your foot falls asleep and wakes up. It's not magic. It's ions doing their job.

When I first heard an old song in a new track, I thought sampling had to be as simple as cutting a line and dropping it in. It isn't. The music might look effortless, but there's a lot of fiddling underneath. You're not just stealing four seconds of someone else's record and calling it done.

I've started seeing this the same way a chef uses a family recipe: you keep the recognizable part, but you change the seasoning until it fits what you're making. A producer might find a phrase from an old record, lower it, stretch it, cut it into smaller pieces, and loop a bit of it. Sometimes the sample is just a beat or a hum. Other times it's a whole vocal line. The point isn't exactness. It's making the old song feel like it belongs in the new track.

The part people overlook is permission. If you use a recognizable piece of somebody's recording, you usually have to ask the owner and the original artist, and often pay for the right to use it. That can take weeks, and it's where a good idea can get stuck. I've been thinking about this because I keep noticing how much work hides behind a two-second loop. I remember reading about artists arguing over how much of a song counts as too much, and the whole thing can become a legal headache. I'm not a lawyer, so I keep my advice practical: if you plan to release it, talk to the people who hold the rights before you fall in love with a loop.

I think the best samples are the ones that don't announce themselves. They sit under the new track, give it a feeling of history, and let listeners recognize something without making the song a museum display. That's the trick. You borrow enough to connect the old world to the new one, but not so much that the listener is just hearing a tribute act. A sample is a conversation between two eras, not a copy.

For me, the appeal is the little moment where an old line suddenly sounds brand new. It's not about being clever. It's about making a memory from someone's past feel like it belongs in your present. Which is why sampling can be both a technical craft and a kind of time travel. If I were making a track, I'd pick one short piece, clear it early, and only then start stacking beats around it.

I used to think headaches were just my brain hurting, but it's not the brain itself. When I get one, the pressure builds in my temples. I'm pretty sure a lot of the pain comes from the blood vessels and the sensitive tissue around the skull reacting, kind of like the feeling when you're dehydrated or haven't slept. I don't know if mine are triggered by screen time, low food intake, or both, but I've noticed that when I sit too still or skip a meal, the ache shows up within a couple of hours. What helps me is drinking water, getting a little movement, and dark quiet for twenty minutes. Sometimes I just lie down in the dark and the dull throb fades. I'm not going to pretend I understand all of it, but I'd rather know what triggers mine than just wait for it to pass.

I can’t tell you if the food was good because we never got to eat. We arrived Sunday at 7:20 p.m. and picked this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and thought it'd be easy. We entered our names in their useless digital waitlist and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff said we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15. It was a party of two, and they offered no fixes. If the wait stretches that far past payment, tell people up front so our night isn’t completely wasted. It was a mess. I’d give it zero stars if that were an option.

I was there Friday around 4:30 p.m. and, which was a pleasant surprise, there was no line at all. The bill for two came out at about $130, and that felt pretty steep. Before going I was figuring the price would be on par with a steakhouse, but afterward I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one. I was disappointed that steak wasn't on the menu. At that price I'd assumed there'd be a steak option. The meat side had lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are the sort of things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less.

The seafood station is where I'd point you. It had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't seen rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The catch was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next one that I didn't want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I stuck to the legs.

The Asian food wasn't much of a stand-out either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. For dessert there was gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They had fresh juices too, though I didn't try any.

I'd call it acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. If the line is long I'd probably think twice.

Four and a half stars. Keeping it.

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key repeats now and then, so example becomes eexample and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself. They were brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar closer to the middle.

I’ve spent most of my life in Vegas, at least in the under-21 part of it, so I’d seen plenty of shows before I was old enough to gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally got to see. It was mixed, maybe a little worse than mixed.

The circular stage is the smart part. You’re looking down into it, so no matter where you sit, you get a fair view. That’s not common in Vegas. A few acts are impressive too, like the strength stuff, the aerialists, and the divers. Those performers are athletes, no question. A lot of it brought Cirque du Soleil to mind. Not exactly a rip-off, but if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen similar feats, often with more clarity.

That clarity is what’s missing here. What’s the story? There’s a dream, maybe. A guy. Water. It lands as a pile of pretty images, but the show never tells you what it means to say. There’s also too much going on at once. Too many people, too many elements, and wow moments stacked on top of each other. A smaller production would hit harder. This felt like that stereotypical Vegas spectacle move, where more has to be better, so they crammed everything in.

One note, if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, there’s a deal, $99 instead of the usual $125. Helps. Would I go again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay to see it twice. Beyond a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else in the house was either. A few friends liked it, though, so if you haven’t seen it yet, it may be worth a look. Just don’t expect to walk away overwhelmed.

About two years ago, I called Rockmount Ranch Wear and ordered two shirts for my father. They never showed up because the sales representative miscopied our address. She had written our street number as a 1 instead of a 7, so the package went to 5401 instead of 5407. The people living there took it to the local UPS store for return, then it vanished. We only found out weeks later. While that was being disputed, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original pair. Their owner took over then. He admitted it had been sent to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts were sent back. He also said it was partly our fault for not being friendly enough to the residents at 5401, just four doors away. We put a dispute on the original charge with our credit-card company and eventually got the money back as a credit.
